content: Cefadroxil is a cephalosporin antibiotic approved by the FDA for treating urinary tract infections caused by Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, and Klebsiella species. It is also indicated for skin and skin structure infections caused by staphylococci and/or streptococci, as well as pharyngitis and/or tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci). Common adverse reactions include gastrointestinal upset, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. For pediatric patients, the recommended daily dosage for urinary tract infections is 30 mg/kg/day, divided into doses every 12 hours. For pharyngitis, tonsillitis, and impetigo, the same dosage can be administered as a single dose or divided into doses every 12 hours. For other skin and skin structure infections, the dosage is also 30 mg/kg/day, divided into doses every 12 hours. In cases of Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infections, therapy should be continued for at least 10 days. Cefadroxil monohydrate is contraindicated in patients with known allergies to cephalosporins. Before initiating therapy, a thorough history of hypersensitivity reactions to cefadroxil, cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs should be obtained. Caution is advised when administering cefadroxil to penicillin-sensitive patients due to documented cross-sensitivity among beta-lactam antibiotics, which may occur in up to 10% of patients with a history of penicillin allergy. If an allergic reaction occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately. Severe hypersensitivity reactions may require treatment with epinephrine and other emergency measures, such as oxygen, intravenous fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids, pressor amines, and airway management. Pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefadroxil, and can range from mild to life-threatening. This diagnosis should be considered in patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic administration. Antibacterial therapy alters the normal flora of the colon, potentially allowing overgrowth of Clostridium difficile. Studies indicate that a toxin produced by C. difficile is a primary cause of antibiotic-associated colitis. Once pseudomembranous colitis is diagnosed, appropriate therapeutic measures should be initiated. Mild cases typically respond to discontinuation of the drug alone, while moderate to severe cases may require fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, and treatment with an antibacterial agent effective against C. difficile. Adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Allergic reactions such as rash, urticaria, angioedema, and pruritus have been observed, typically resolving upon discontinuation of the drug. Rarely, anaphylaxis has been reported. Other reactions include hepatic dysfunction (e.g., cholestasis, elevated transaminases), genital pruritus, genital moniliasis, vaginitis, transient neutropenia, fever, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, idiosyncratic hepatic failure, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, serum sickness, and arthralgia. Cephalosporins, including cefadroxil, have also been associated with toxic epidermal necrolysis, abdominal pain, superinfection, renal dysfunction, toxic nephropathy, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, hemorrhage, prolonged prothrombin time, positive Coombs’ test, increased BUN, increased creatinine, elevated alkaline phosphatase, elevated AST/ALT, elevated bilirubin, elevated LDH, eosinophilia, pancytopenia, and neutropenia. Seizures have been reported, particularly in patients with renal impairment when dosage adjustments were not made. If seizures occur, the drug should be discontinued, and anticonvulsant therapy may be administered if clinically indicated. Cefadroxil is rapidly absorbed after oral administration. Following single doses of 500 mg and 1000 mg, average peak serum concentrations are approximately 16 mcg/mL and 28 mcg/mL, respectively. Measurable levels persist for 12 hours post-administration. Over 90% of the drug is excreted unchanged in the urine within 24 hours, with peak urine concentrations of approximately 1800 mcg/mL following a single 500 mg oral dose. Dosage increases generally result in proportional increases in urinary concentrations. After a 1 g dose, urinary antibiotic concentrations remain above the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) for susceptible urinary pathogens for 20 to 22 hours. Cefadroxil is substantially excreted by the kidneys, and dosage adjustments are necessary for patients with renal impairment to prevent drug accumulation. In adults, the initial dose is 1000 mg, followed by maintenance doses of 500 mg at intervals based on creatinine clearance rates. Patients with creatinine clearance rates over 50 mL/min can be treated as those with normal renal function. Cefadroxil is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA. Animal reproduction studies in mice and rats at doses up to 11 times the human dose have shown no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Therefore, cefadroxil should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. It has not been studied for use during labor and delivery, and caution is advised when administering it to nursing mothers. In geriatric patients, no overall differences in safety were observed compared to younger patients in clinical trials. However, elderly patients are more likely to have decreased renal function, necessitating careful dose selection and monitoring of renal function. Cefadroxil is supplied as white to off-white, film-coated, oval-shaped tablets with specific markings. Tablets should be stored at 20°–25°C (68°–77°F). There is limited information regarding its administration, monitoring, IV compatibility, and postmarketing experience. Additionally, no specific guidance exists for its use in pediatric, gender-specific, racial, hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised populations. Alcohol interaction with cefadroxil has not been established, and patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol consumption while on this medication.
